section.title: Cleansing of Skin Diseases and Mildew
section.sectionRationale: Chapter thirteen diagnosed disease; this chapter provides the ritual for restoring a healed person to the camp and to worship, along with the parallel law for a house contaminated with mildew, closing the purity regulations concerning skin disease.
section.thesis: God provides an elaborate, joyful ritual for restoring a healed person to full community life, two birds, cedar, scarlet yarn, and hyssop, followed by sacrifices with blood and oil applied to ear, thumb, and toe just as in priestly ordination, teaching that restoration to fellowship with God and His people is as carefully provided for as exclusion was required.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the cleansing ritual with two birds outside the camp; the eighth day sacrifices restoring full access to the sanctuary; the provision for the poor; and the parallel law for a house contaminated with mildew.

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“This is the law for the one afflicted with a skin disease on the day of his cleansing, when he is brought to the priest.
The priest is to go outside the camp to examine him, and if the skin disease of the afflicted person has healed,
the priest shall order that two live clean birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and {{ezov|hyssop}} be brought for the one to be cleansed.
Then the priest shall command that one of the birds be slaughtered over fresh water in a clay pot.
And he is to take the live bird together with the cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop, and dip them into the blood of the bird that was slaughtered over the fresh water.
Seven times he shall sprinkle the one to be cleansed of the skin disease. Then he shall pronounce him clean and release the live bird into the open field.

The one being cleansed must wash his clothes, shave off all his hair, and bathe with water; then he will be ceremonially clean. Afterward, he may enter the camp, but he must remain outside his tent for seven days.
On the seventh day he must shave off all his hair, his head, his beard, his eyebrows, and the rest of his hair. He must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water, and he will be clean.

units.label: The eighth day
units.note: blood and oil on ear, thumb, and toe

verses.text: On the eighth day he is to bring two unblemished male lambs, an unblemished ewe lamb a year old, a grain offering of three-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with olive oil, and one log of olive oil.
The priest who performs the cleansing shall present the one to be cleansed, together with these offerings, before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.
Then the priest is to take one of the male lambs and present it as a guilt offering, along with the log of olive oil; and he must wave them as a wave offering before the LORD.
Then he is to slaughter the lamb in the sanctuary area where the sin offering and burnt offering are slaughtered. Like the sin offering, the guilt offering belongs to the priest; it is most holy.
The priest is to take some of the blood from the guilt offering and put it on the right earlobe of the one to be cleansed, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.
Then the priest shall take some of the log of olive oil, pour it into his left palm,
dip his right forefinger into the oil in his left palm, and sprinkle some of the oil with his finger seven times before the LORD.

And the priest is to put some of the oil remaining in his palm on the right earlobe of the one to be cleansed, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot, on top of the blood of the guilt offering.
The rest of the oil in his palm, the priest is to put on the head of the one to be cleansed, to make {{kipper|atonement}} for him before the LORD.
Then the priest is to sacrifice the sin offering and make atonement for the one to be cleansed from his uncleanness. After that, the priest shall slaughter the burnt offering
and offer it on the altar, with the grain offering, to make atonement for him, and he will be clean.

If, however, the person is poor and cannot afford these offerings, he is to take one male lamb as a guilt offering to be waved to make atonement for him, along with a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with olive oil for a grain offering, a log of olive oil,
and two turtledoves or two young pigeons, whichever he can afford, one to be a sin offering and the other a burnt offering.
On the eighth day he is to bring them for his cleansing to the priest at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting before the LORD.
The priest shall take the lamb for the guilt offering, along with the log of olive oil, and wave them as a wave offering before the LORD.

And after he slaughters the lamb for the guilt offering, the priest is to take some of the blood of the guilt offering and put it on the right earlobe of the one to be cleansed, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.
Then the priest is to pour some of the oil into his left palm
and sprinkle with his right forefinger some of the oil in his left palm seven times before the LORD.

The priest shall also put some of the oil in his palm on the right earlobe of the one to be cleansed, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot, on the same places as the blood of the guilt offering.
The rest of the oil in his palm, the priest is to put on the head of the one to be cleansed, to make atonement for him before the LORD.
Then he must sacrifice the turtledoves or young pigeons, whichever he can afford,
one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, together with the grain offering. In this way the priest will make atonement before the LORD for the one to be cleansed.
This is the law for someone who has a skin disease and cannot afford the cost of his cleansing.”
Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron,
“When you enter the land of Canaan, which I am giving you as your possession, and I put a contamination of mildew into a house in that land,
the owner of the house shall come and tell the priest, ‘Something like mildew has appeared in my house.’
The priest must order that the house be cleared before he enters it to examine the mildew, so that nothing in the house will become unclean. After this, the priest shall go in to inspect the house.
He is to examine the house, and if the mildew on the walls consists of green or red depressions that appear to be beneath the surface of the wall,
the priest shall go outside the doorway of the house and close it up for seven days.
On the seventh day the priest is to return and inspect the house. If the mildew has spread on the walls,
he must order that the contaminated stones be pulled out and thrown into an unclean place outside the city.
And he shall have the inside of the house scraped completely and the plaster that is scraped off dumped into an unclean place outside the city.
So different stones must be obtained to replace the contaminated ones, as well as additional mortar to replaster the house.
If the mildew reappears in the house after the stones have been torn out and the house has been scraped and replastered,
the priest must come and inspect it. If the mildew has spread in the house, it is a destructive mildew; the house is unclean.
It must be torn down with its stones, its timbers, and all its plaster, and taken outside the city to an unclean place.
Anyone who enters the house during any of the days that it is closed up will be unclean until evening.
And anyone who sleeps in the house or eats in it must wash his clothes.
If, however, the priest comes and inspects it, and the mildew has not spread after the house has been replastered, he shall pronounce the house clean, because the mildew is gone.
He is to take two birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop to purify the house;
and he shall slaughter one of the birds over fresh water in a clay pot.
Then he shall take the cedar wood, the hyssop, the scarlet yarn, and the live bird, dip them in the blood of the slaughtered bird and the fresh water, and sprinkle the house seven times.
And he shall cleanse the house with the bird's blood, the fresh water, the live bird, the cedar wood, the hyssop, and the scarlet yarn.
Finally, he is to release the live bird into the open fields outside the city. In this way he will make atonement for the house, and it will be clean.
This is the law for any infectious skin disease, for a scaly outbreak,
for mildew in clothing or in a house,
and for a swelling, rash, or spot,
to determine when something is clean or unclean. This is the law regarding skin diseases and mildew.”

ezov.gloss: Hyssop, a small bushy plant used throughout Scripture for sprinkling blood or water in cleansing rituals, including the Passover, Exodus 12:22, and later invoked by David's plea, purge me with hyssop, Psalm 51:7, as a symbol of thorough cleansing from sin.

kipper.gloss: To atone, to cover. Even after the disease itself had visibly healed, atonement still had to be made before the person was declared fully clean, showing that restoration to community and to worship required more than physical healing alone.

basic.context: Where chapter thirteen diagnosed disease, this chapter provides the joyful ritual for restoring a healed person to full community life. Two birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop are used outside the camp, followed eight days later by sacrifices whose blood and oil are applied to the healed person's ear, thumb, and toe, echoing exactly the ordination of priests. The chapter closes with the same careful pattern applied to a house contaminated with mildew.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes Israel's actual old covenant ritual for restoring a healed person and a contaminated house to cleanness; it is not a pattern for Christian healing or house blessing rituals today. Its abiding truth is that God cares as much about restoration and homecoming as He does about the exclusion that disease required, and that being clean before God, then as now, is never merely a private matter but restores full participation in community.
basic.originalLanguages: The ritual uses ezov, hyssop, the same plant used at the first Passover to apply blood to Israel's doorposts, and later invoked by David's own plea for cleansing from sin, purge me with hyssop, Psalm 51:7. Even after physical healing was confirmed, kaphar, atonement, still had to be made, showing that the disease's ceremonial weight went beyond mere physical illness.
basic.typology: That the healed leper receives blood and oil on ear, thumb, and toe, the very ritual used to ordain priests in chapters eight and nine, suggests that being restored from this defiling condition returns a person to something like the priestly, worshiping community in full. The two birds, one slain and one released alive carrying the blood, anticipate the pattern later fulfilled in the two goats of the Day of Atonement, chapter sixteen, one goat slain and one sent away bearing sin.
basic.christ: The hyssop used here recalls both the first Passover, Exodus 12:22, and points to Christ, our Passover Lamb, whose blood truly cleanses, echoed when hyssop appears again at the crucifixion, John 19:29. As the healed person was restored not only physically but ceremonially, fully welcomed back into worship, so Christ's cleansing restores sinners not merely to healing but to full fellowship and priestly access to God, 1 Peter 2:9.
basic.god: God's law provided joyful, thorough restoration for the very people this system had required to be excluded, showing that exclusion was never His final intention but a temporary measure protecting the community's holiness until healing came. His care extends to providing an accessible path for the poor, exactly as with earlier offerings, proving restoration was never withheld for lack of means.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 12:22 describes hyssop used to apply the Passover lamb's blood to the doorposts. Psalm 51:7 has David plead, purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean, applying this ritual language to the cleansing of sin itself. John 19:29 records hyssop lifted to Jesus on the cross, tying His final moments to this whole pattern of cleansing.
basic.oneStory: This chapter shows a God who provides thorough, joyful restoration for those healed from a defiling disease, welcoming them back fully into community and worship, never leaving exclusion as His last word. It anticipates Christ, our true Passover Lamb, whose blood, applied like the hyssop of this ritual, cleanses sinners fully and restores them to complete fellowship with God.

context.literary:
Leviticus 14 falls into three laws and a closing summary. Verses 1 to 20 give the cleansing of a healed person; verses 21 to 32 give the same rite scaled for the poor; verses 33 to 53 turn to a house with mildew; and verses 54 to 57 sum up chapters 13 and 14 together as "the law regarding skin diseases and mildew."

The first law is carefully staged in time and space. On the first day the priest goes out to the person "outside the camp," verse 3, and performs the rite of the two birds. The person then washes, shaves and bathes, and may "enter the camp," but "must remain outside his tent for seven days," verse 8. On the seventh day he shaves and washes again. On the eighth day he is brought "before the LORD at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting," verse 11. The movement runs from outside the camp, to inside the camp but outside his own tent, to the doorway of God's tent. Chapter 13 drove him out step by step; chapter 14 brings him home step by step.

The pattern of seven days followed by an eighth deliberately recalls the ordination of the priests, who remained at the Tent for seven days, Leviticus 8:33, and began their service "on the eighth day," Leviticus 9:1. The blood and oil on ear, thumb and toe, verses 14 to 18, make the echo unmistakable.

The chapter is framed by the same unusual ingredients. Two birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn and hyssop appear at the start, verse 4, and again for the house, verse 49, so the rite for a person and the rite for a building bracket everything in between. The poor man's section repeats the rich man's almost word for word, so that the reader sees his cleansing is not a lesser version but the same one.
context.historical:
The ingredients of the bird rite were ordinary things of Israel's world. Cedar was a fragrant, durable wood; the scarlet yarn was wool dyed crimson; and hyssop was a small bushy plant suitable for sprinkling, as at the Passover, Exodus 12:22. Solomon's wisdom spanned "the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop growing in the wall," 1 Kings 4:33, so the rite joins the grandest and the humblest of plants. The same three items appear in the rite of the red heifer for cleansing from contact with the dead, Numbers 19:6. The "fresh water" of verse 5 is water from a spring or stream, not standing water from a cistern, as the BSB footnote indicates.

The cost of full cleansing was considerable: three lambs, three tenths of an ephah of fine flour, and a log of oil, verse 10, which the BSB footnotes estimate at about six and a half litres of flour and a third of a litre of oil. The poor man's provision, one lamb, a tenth of an ephah, and two birds, verses 21 and 22, was still a real offering, but within reach.

The law for houses begins, "When you enter the land of Canaan, which I am giving you," verse 34. It looks ahead from tents in the wilderness to stone houses with plastered walls. The priest's instruction to empty the house before he enters, verse 36, protects the owner's goods from being declared unclean, a practical kindness. Contaminated stones and plaster are dumped in "an unclean place outside the city," verses 40 and 41, the counterpart for a house of the leper's dwelling outside the camp.

The guilt offering stands out. It normally answered a breach against the LORD's holy things, Leviticus 5:15, and here it is the first sacrifice, its blood applied to the person. Whatever the precise reason, the person's long absence from the sanctuary was treated as a matter requiring reparation.
context.canonical:
The chapter weaves together threads that run through the whole Bible. Its hyssop reaches back to the Passover, Exodus 12:22, and forward to the red heifer, Numbers 19:18, and to Moses' sprinkling of the covenant scroll and the people with "water, scarlet wool, and hyssop," Hebrews 9:19. David, confessing his sin, prays in the language of this chapter: "Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean," Psalm 51:7.

Its two birds anticipate the two goats of the Day of Atonement, one slain and one sent away alive into the wilderness, Leviticus 16:10 and 16:21-22. Its ear, thumb and toe repeat the ordination of Aaron and his sons, Exodus 29:20 and Leviticus 8:23-24.

The later histories show the law in action and beyond it. Naaman's sevenfold washing in the Jordan, 2 Kings 5:14, echoes the sevenfold sprinkling of verse 7, and the prophet's word achieves what the priest's rite could only declare. Zechariah pictures a curse that enters a house and "will remain inside his house and destroy it, down to its timbers and stones," Zechariah 5:4, the language of verse 45 turned into a prophecy of judgment on the unfaithful.

The Gospels show Jesus sending cleansed lepers to perform this very rite. He tells one to "present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them," Mark 1:44, and ten are cleansed on the way to the priests, Luke 17:14. At the cross a stalk of hyssop lifts sour wine to His mouth, John 19:29. The New Testament then describes believers as those who have been washed and consecrated, a people made "a kingdom, priests to His God and Father," Revelation 1:6, and a house built of "living stones," 1 Peter 2:5.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wanted Israel to know that the exclusion described in chapter 13 was not meant to be permanent. God provided a road back, and it was marked out as carefully as the road out. Every stage, from the field outside the camp to the entrance of the Tent, is described so that no healed person need wonder whether he truly belonged again.

He also wanted Israel to understand that restoration was God's work, not a formality. The priest goes out to the person, examines him, and performs the rites; the one being cleansed contributes washing, shaving and offerings, but the declaration and the atonement come through God's appointed mediator. Even the house, the family's shelter and inheritance in the land, is placed under the same careful discernment, because the land and its homes were God's gift, verse 34.

Finally, he meant the rite to say something about the person restored. The blood and oil applied as at the priests' ordination, and the oil poured on his head, set the healed Israelite apart again for God's service with ear, hand and foot. The first hearers were meant to see that the one who returns is not a second class member of the camp, but one consecrated afresh.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter prescribes rites for Israel: birds, cedar, scarlet yarn, hyssop, shaving, washing, sacrifices and the inspection of houses. None of it is binding on the church, and it offers no model for Christian healing services or house blessings. The sacrifices are fulfilled in Christ, whose blood "cleanses us from all sin," 1 John 1:7.

The Gospels record Jesus sending healed men to carry out this rite, Mark 1:44 and Luke 17:14. That is a description of His honouring the law while it was still in force, and of His desire that the priests themselves should witness what He had done, not an instruction for His followers to seek priestly certification.

What does carry forward is the shape of restoration. When someone has been separated from the fellowship of God's people and is restored, the restoration should be as clear and wholehearted as the separation was, 2 Corinthians 2:7-8 in the case of a repentant brother. The chapter also teaches that God's provision of cleansing is never priced out of the reach of the poor, and that worship involves the whole person, hearing, acting and walking, Romans 12:1.

debates.question: Why does the healed leper receive the same ear, thumb, and toe ritual used at priestly ordination, chapters 8 and 14:14?

views.label: A restoration to full covenant participation
views.case: Many interpreters see this deliberate echo as marking the healed person's full return to covenant life and worship, using the same symbolic consecration of hearing, doing, and walking applied to priests. The whole nation was called 'a kingdom of priests,' Exodus 19:6, and the rite reinstates one member of that priestly people.

views.label: A demonstration of the completeness of the person's cleansing
views.case: Others emphasize that the shared ritual pattern primarily communicates thoroughness, that this cleansing, like ordination, left no part of the person untouched by the process, rather than implying any priestly status. The extremities stand for the whole body, from head to foot.

debates.bearing: The two readings work together. The rite touches the whole person, and in doing so it returns him to the priestly people of God, not as a priest at the altar, but as one set apart again to hear, act and walk before the LORD.

debates.question: What does the release of the live bird into the open field signify, verse 7?

views.label: The removal of impurity
views.case: Many read the live bird, dipped in the blood of the slain bird, as carrying the uncleanness away, much as the scapegoat carries Israel's sins into the wilderness, Leviticus 16:21-22. The same rite is used for the house, verse 53, where the bird's flight plainly signals that the contamination is gone.

views.label: A picture of the person's own freedom and new life
views.case: Others see in the bird that flies free, marked by the blood of death, a picture of the healed person himself, released from a living death and returned to the open world. Many Christian readers, from the church fathers on, have seen in the two birds a figure of Christ's death and resurrection.

debates.bearing: The text does not explain the rite, and both ideas may be present. The primary thought, supported by the parallel with Leviticus 16 and with the house, is removal: what made the person unclean is sent far away. Christian reflection on death and new life is fair as application, as long as it is held more lightly than the text's own logic.

study.originalLanguages:
The "fresh water" of verses 5, 6 and 50 to 52 is literally "living water," mayim chayyim, as the BSB footnote says: water from a flowing source. The phrase carries its meaning into the prophets and the Gospels. The LORD calls Himself "the fountain of living water," Jeremiah 2:13; Zechariah sees "living water" flowing out from Jerusalem, Zechariah 14:8; and Jesus offers the Samaritan woman "living water," John 4:10, and promises that "streams of living water" will flow from those who believe, John 7:38.

When the priest will "purify the house," verse 49, and "cleanse the house," verse 52, the verb is the intensive stem of chata', the root of the word for sin. In this stem it means to purify or cleanse from sin's defilement. It is the very verb of Psalm 51:7, "Purify me with hyssop." David takes the language of the leper's and the house's cleansing and applies it to his own guilt.

The first sacrifice is an asham, "guilt offering," verse 12. In Leviticus 5:15 the asham answers an unfaithful act "against any of the LORD's holy things," and it carries the idea of reparation or compensation. Its use here, for a person who has done no stated wrong, shows how seriously the law treats a long absence from the holy. Isaiah uses the same word of the Servant: "when His soul is made a guilt offering," Isaiah 53:10.

The blood is applied to the tenuk, the right earlobe, the bohen, thumb, and the big toe, verse 14. These are the same terms used for the ordination of Aaron and his sons, Exodus 29:20 and Leviticus 8:23-24. The oil is then put "on top of the blood," verse 17, and the remainder on the head, verse 18. In Aaron's ordination anointing oil was poured on his head, Leviticus 8:12, which Psalm 133:2 remembers as oil "running down on the beard, running down Aaron's beard."

The live bird is "released," verse 7, from shalach, to send away, the same verb used for sending the scapegoat into the wilderness, Leviticus 16:21-22. In verse 34 God speaks in the first person: "I put a contamination of mildew into a house." The verb natan, to give or put, is the same as in "the land of Canaan, which I am giving you." The giver of the house is sovereign even over its decay.

Finally, verse 53 says the priest will "make atonement for the house." A house cannot sin or repent. The verb kipper here plainly means to purge or cleanse from defilement, which sheds light on its use for the person in verses 18 to 20: atonement in these chapters restores what uncleanness has spoiled.

typology.type: The two birds, one slain over living water and one released alive, Leviticus 14:4-7
typology.fulfillment: One bird dies, and the other, dipped in its blood, flies free into the open field, as the person is pronounced clean. Many Christian readers have seen here a figure of Christ, who 'was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification,' Romans 4:25. The escalation is that in Christ one person is both the one who dies and the one who lives, and His people are raised with Him to 'walk in newness of life,' Romans 6:4. The type falls short because two different birds were needed and the rite had to be repeated for every case; Christ's death and resurrection happen once for all.

typology.type: Blood and oil on the right ear, thumb and big toe, Leviticus 14:14-17
typology.fulfillment: The rite that ordained priests is applied to an ordinary Israelite restored from uncleanness, marking hearing, doing and walking as belonging to God. In Christ every believer is cleansed by His blood and made part of 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9, and Christ has 'made us to be a kingdom, priests to His God and Father,' Revelation 1:5-6. The escalation is that the consecration is not limited to a single restored person or a single priestly family but extends to all God's people, who offer their bodies 'as living sacrifices,' Romans 12:1. The type falls short because the blood of a lamb could mark the skin but not renew the heart.

typology.type: The oil poured on the head of the one cleansed, Leviticus 14:18
typology.fulfillment: The healed Israelite receives oil on his head, recalling the anointing of Aaron, Leviticus 8:12. Jesus is the Anointed One in the fullest sense: 'God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power,' Acts 10:38, and He began His ministry announcing, 'He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor,' Luke 4:18. Those joined to Him share His anointing, 2 Corinthians 1:21-22 and 1 John 2:20. The escalation moves from oil on the skin to the Spirit in the heart. The type falls short because the oil marked a restoration the person had to wait for; the Spirit is God's pledge of what is to come.

typology.type: The house whose infected stones are replaced, Leviticus 14:40-45
typology.fulfillment: A house with spreading mildew has its stones replaced, and if the corruption returns it is torn down entirely. Jesus spoke of the temple in those terms: 'not one stone here will be left on another,' Matthew 24:2. God's new house is built of believers, 'living stones' being built into 'a spiritual house,' 1 Peter 2:5, and 'a dwelling place for God in His Spirit,' Ephesians 2:22. The escalation is from a house cleansed to a house that is itself holy. The type falls short because new stones could still be infected; God's new house is kept by Christ, who is 'faithful as the Son over God's house,' Hebrews 3:6.

study.christ:
The chapter begins with a detail easily missed: "The priest is to go outside the camp to examine him," verse 3. The healed person cannot come in until someone comes out. That is the movement of the gospel. "The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost," Luke 19:10, and He went "outside the city gate" to sanctify His people by His own blood, Hebrews 13:12.

It leads to Christ through His own use of the law. When Jesus cleansed a leper, He told him, "go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them," Mark 1:44. The offering Moses prescribed is Leviticus 14. Jesus wanted the priests, performing the birds, the cedar and the hyssop, to face the fact that a man declared unclean had been made clean by the word of Jesus. The rite became a witness to the one it pointed toward.

It leads to Christ by pattern. The slain bird and the living bird, the blood of death that sets the living free, give a picture that Christians have long seen fulfilled in the death and resurrection of Jesus. The hyssop, which in this chapter sprinkles cleansing blood, appears once more at the cross, when a sponge is lifted to His lips on a stalk of hyssop, John 19:29. The guilt offering whose blood is placed on the restored man is the very word Isaiah uses for the Servant whose soul is made "a guilt offering," Isaiah 53:10.

It leads to Christ as the one who consecrates. The ear, thumb and toe of the healed man are marked like a priest's, and the oil is poured on his head. The Anointed One, Jesus, takes cleansed people and makes them priests, Revelation 1:5-6, whose ears hear His word, whose hands serve, and whose feet walk in His ways. And because the rite includes a full provision for the poor, verses 21 to 32, it anticipates the one anointed "to preach good news to the poor," Luke 4:18.

It leads to Christ in the house. The laws for a contaminated house anticipate God's judgment on a temple that would not be cleansed, Matthew 24:2, and His building of a new house from living stones, 1 Peter 2:5.

A caution keeps this honest. Leviticus 14 is first a real rite for a real people, and not every detail, the cedar, the scarlet, the clay pot, needs a Christian meaning. The New Testament does not interpret the birds explicitly. What is certain is that Jesus sent healed men to this rite, that His blood accomplishes what its blood pictured, and that in Him the excluded are brought all the way home.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who restores as carefully as He judges. Chapter 13 needed fifty nine verses to describe how a person is examined and excluded; chapter 14 spends fifty seven describing how a person, and a house, are cleansed and received. The proportion itself says something. God's holiness does not delight in exclusion; it makes a road home.

He is a God who comes out. The priest goes outside the camp to the one who cannot come in, verse 3. The initiative in restoration lies with God's appointed mediator, not with the sufferer.

He is patient and thorough. The healed person is not rushed back into the sanctuary. He moves in stages, from field to camp to tent to the entrance of the LORD's house, over eight days. God gives time for restoration to be real, and at every stage there is a clear word about where the person now stands.

He is generous and impartial. The poor man's cleansing, verses 21 to 32, is spelled out at full length, word for word with the rich man's, so that no one could think the poor were cleansed less. The same atonement, the same blood and oil, the same declaration are his.

He is sovereign over the goods of His people. "I put a contamination of mildew into a house," verse 34, is spoken by the same God who says "which I am giving you." He gives the land and the house, and He also governs their decay. His sovereignty is not cold; it comes with a procedure that protects the owner's belongings, verse 36, and seeks to save the house before it is torn down.

He is holy, and His holiness is costly. Even after the disease has healed, blood must be shed and atonement made, verses 18 to 20. Physical recovery is not the same as being fit for God's presence. The chapter holds together His gladness to restore and His insistence that restoration come through sacrifice.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to marvel that God consecrates the restored rather than merely tolerating them, to offer ear, hand and foot to Him, and to welcome back those whom He has cleansed with the same wholeheartedness He shows.

crossReferences.note: Moses puts the ram's blood on the right earlobe, thumb and big toe of Aaron and his sons at their ordination. Leviticus 14:14 applies the identical rite to the healed person, placing his restoration in the language of consecration to God's service.

Cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet wool are thrown onto the burning red heifer, whose ashes cleanse from contact with the dead. The same three items in Leviticus 14:4 tie the leper's cleansing to cleansing from death, the reality his disease so vividly resembled.

On the Day of Atonement one goat is slain and the other is sent away alive into the wilderness bearing Israel's iniquities. The two birds of Leviticus 14:4-7, one slain and one released, present the same pattern on a smaller scale for a single person.

David prays, 'Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean,' using the same verb as the purification of the house in Leviticus 14:49. He asks God to do for his sin what the hyssop rite did for the leper and the house.

Naaman dips himself seven times in the Jordan and his flesh becomes 'like that of a little child.' The sevenfold washing echoes the sevenfold sprinkling of Leviticus 14:7, but here God heals directly through the prophet's word.

Jesus sends the leper He has healed to 'present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them.' The offering is the one laid out in Leviticus 14, and the priests who perform it become witnesses to Jesus' power.

The Servant's soul is made 'a guilt offering,' the same term as the asham whose blood is placed on the healed person in Leviticus 14:12-14. What the lamb provided for one leper, the Servant provides for many.

At the making of the covenant Moses sprinkled the book and the people using 'water, scarlet wool, and hyssop.' Hebrews gathers the ingredients of Leviticus 14 into its argument that everything under the law was purified with blood, pointing to Christ's better sacrifice.

Believers are 'living stones' being built into 'a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood.' The two halves of Leviticus 14, the restored priest-like person and the house rebuilt with new stones, meet in Peter's picture of the church.

Christ 'has released us from our sins by His blood' and 'made us to be a kingdom, priests.' The movement of Leviticus 14 from uncleanness, through blood, to consecration with ear, thumb and toe reaches its full scope in the people of God.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a man and woman at home in God's presence, and then tells of their being sent out of the garden, eastward and away. From that point the great question of Scripture is how exiles come home. Leviticus 13 showed a person sent outside the camp, an Adam in miniature. Leviticus 14 shows the way back.

In the story of Israel, the chapter gives a pattern for homecoming. The priest goes out; blood is shed; living water is used; the one outside is washed, waits, and then is brought in stages to the door of God's house, where he is consecrated like a priest. The pattern also reaches to houses in the promised land, since God's concern extends to the homes and inheritance of His people.

The nation itself would later need that road. Israel's sins led to exile, and the prophets promised a cleansing on a national scale: "I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean," Ezekiel 36:25. David had already prayed in the chapter's own words for a clean heart, Psalm 51:7 and 51:10.

In Christ the road home is opened for good. He comes outside the camp to the unclean, He sends the healed to the priests as a testimony, and at the cross the hyssop is lifted to His mouth as He becomes the guilt offering for many. He rises, and those joined to Him are cleansed, anointed with His Spirit and made a royal priesthood. The house of God is rebuilt from living stones.

The story ends where Leviticus 14 points. The new Jerusalem has a river of "the water of life," Revelation 22:1, the true living water. God's people "have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb," Revelation 7:14, and they serve Him as priests. No one waits outside the camp or outside his tent any longer. The eighth day has dawned, and the exiles are home.

quiz.q: What materials are used in the initial cleansing ritual performed outside the camp for a healed person?

options.text: Two live clean birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop.
options.note: Verse 4 lists exactly these materials for the initial ritual.

options.text: Oil and frankincense only.
options.note: Oil is used later in the eighth day ritual, verses 15 to 18; the initial ritual specifically requires birds, cedar, scarlet yarn, and hyssop.

options.text: A bull and a ram.
options.note: Larger animals appear in the eighth day sacrifices, verse 10, but the initial outside the camp ritual uses birds, not a bull or ram.

options.text: No specific materials are listed.
options.note: Verse 4 gives an explicit list of materials.

quiz.q: Where is the blood of the guilt offering applied to the healed person on the eighth day?

options.text: The right earlobe, the thumb of the right hand, and the big toe of the right foot.
options.note: Verse 14 specifies this exact application, identical to the ordination ritual of chapter 8.

options.text: Only the forehead.
options.note: The ritual specified here applies blood to ear, thumb, and toe, not the forehead.

options.text: The hands only.
options.note: The blood is applied to ear, thumb, and toe together, not the hands alone.

options.text: No blood application is described.
options.note: Verse 14 explicitly describes this application.

quiz.q: What provision does this chapter make for a healed person who is too poor to afford the standard offerings?

options.text: One male lamb as a guilt offering, and two turtledoves or two young pigeons for the sin and burnt offerings.
options.note: Verses 21 to 22 describe this scaled down provision for the poor.

options.text: He is exempt from any offering.
options.note: The law provides an accessible alternative rather than an exemption from all offerings.

options.text: He must wait until he can afford the full offering.
options.note: The provision allows immediate cleansing at a reduced cost, not a delay.

options.text: No provision is made for the poor.
options.note: Verses 21 to 32 give an extended, detailed provision for the poor.

quiz.q: What must happen to a house if mildew reappears after the contaminated stones have been removed and it has been replastered?

options.text: The house must be torn down completely, with its stones, timbers, and plaster taken outside the city.
options.note: Verses 43 to 45 describe this final measure for a house with destructive, persistent mildew.

options.text: The house is simply abandoned but left standing.
options.note: Verse 45 explicitly requires the house to be torn down and its materials removed, not merely abandoned.

options.text: The homeowner must live in it despite the danger.
options.note: The text requires the house's destruction, not continued habitation.

options.text: Nothing further is required.
options.note: Verses 43 to 45 give an explicit, further requirement.

quiz.q: What happens to the live bird at the end of both the person's and the house's cleansing ritual?

options.text: It is released into the open field or fields outside the city, carrying the blood of the slain bird.
options.note: Verses 7 and 53 both describe releasing the live bird after it has been dipped in the slain bird's blood.

options.text: It is also slaughtered, so that both birds die.
options.note: Only one bird is slaughtered; the other is deliberately kept alive and released, verses 7 and 53.

options.text: It is kept permanently by the priest.
options.note: The text explicitly describes the bird being released, not retained.

options.text: No live bird is used in this ritual.
options.note: Verses 4 to 7 and 49 to 53 explicitly describe the use of a live bird.

questions: This chapter shows God providing an elaborate, joyful ritual to welcome the healed person fully back into community and worship. Is there someone in your life who has been through a hard season and needs you to actively welcome them back, rather than just tolerate their return?

The healed person received the same ear, thumb, and toe ritual used to ordain priests, suggesting a restoration to full, whole hearted worship. What would it look like for you to offer your whole self, hearing, doing, and walking, back to God this week?

Even after physical healing, atonement still had to be made before the person was fully clean. Where in your own life have you experienced healing or improvement in circumstances, yet still need to deal honestly with a deeper spiritual issue underneath?

Hyssop, used here to apply cleansing blood, is the same plant David asked God to use to purge him from sin. When you feel the weight of guilt, do you actually ask God to cleanse you, or do you try to manage the guilt yourself?

God provided a real and generous path back for someone who had been excluded, showing that exclusion was never meant to be permanent. Where might God be calling you to extend that same kind of costly, generous welcome to someone others have written off?

translationNotes.note: The pairing of a slain bird and a live bird released afterward anticipates the two goats of the Day of Atonement in chapter 16, one sacrificed and one sent away, a recurring pattern of substitution and removal in Israel's ritual system.

The application of blood to the right earlobe, thumb, and big toe intentionally mirrors the ordination ritual of chapter 8:23-24, suggesting the healed person's full restoration to whole hearted worship and community life.

I put a contamination of mildew into a house attributes even this affliction to the LORD's sovereign hand, framing house mildew, like skin disease, as ultimately under God's governance rather than random misfortune, though the text does not elaborate a specific moral cause.
